ACEI: Exposure to autocallable notes built on a basket of the largest US stocks, notes that pay income while stocks behave and can return principal early when they rise. The catch is equity like losses if the basket falls past its barrier, an income trade with a cliff edge.
ACSG: Small US growth companies picked with a mix of hands on research and systematic, risk aware portfolio building, led by health care and technology. It hunts future mid sized winners early, so it carries the bigger swings and occasional wipeouts that come with small company investing.
AIOO: Options on the S&P 500 in a maximum protection design set for one year outcome periods: the fund is built to shield against losses on large US stocks in exchange for capped gains. It aims for peace of mind over performance, so strong bull markets will leave it far behind.
ARCM: Very short term bonds, mostly maturing within two years, all investment grade, including mortgage and asset backed securities. It is a cash like holding with a bit more yield, managed carefully to keep price swings tiny for money that cannot afford surprises.
ASIA: Companies across Asia with Japan left out, picked actively, with chipmakers and other technology firms about half the fund and banks next. It is a growth bet on Asia's biggest economies, including China, Taiwan, Korea and India, run by a specialist in the region.
BBCB: Investment grade corporate bonds from across the US market, weighted by size, spanning banks, technology firms, health care companies and other large issuers. It is a plain, broad company bond holding for steady interest, sitting between Treasuries and riskier high yield debt.
BBIB: US Treasury bonds with three to ten years left until they mature, the middle of the government bond curve. It pays steady interest with moderate price swings, moving down when interest rates rise, and serves as a classic core holding for the safer side of a portfolio.
BLDG: Real estate companies around the world, property owners and REITs from developed and emerging markets alike, picked actively. It spreads rent driven income across countries and property types, so it moves with global property markets and local currencies as well as US rates.
BRLN: Floating rate bank loans, debt owed by companies to banks whose interest payments reset as rates change, bought actively rather than by index. Rising rates lift its income instead of hurting it, the mirror image of most bond funds, though the loans carry real credit risk.
BSJW: High yield corporate bonds that all mature in 2032, packaged like a single junk bond with a known end date. It pays junk level interest until then, with more credit risk than investment grade target date funds, and its price swings shrink as 2032 approaches.
CCRP: Corporate bonds picked actively across industries and maturities, company debt from banks, manufacturers, drug makers and others. It works as an income holding that takes company credit risk in exchange for higher interest than government bonds, with managers choosing where the pay is worth the risk.
CRCO: An options income strategy tied to Circle, the company behind a major dollar pegged digital token, using contracts that give indirect exposure to its share price while collecting premiums for monthly payouts. It is an income play on one young, volatile crypto linked stock, with gains capped.
DECU: Options on the S&P 500 set each December for a one year outcome period, cushioning the first 15 percent of losses while leaving gains uncapped after a small starting hurdle. It swaps the usual gain cap for a slow start, a different shape of protection.
DUKZ: A tactical income fund that shifts between other bond funds and cash as its signals dictate, and it can sit mostly in cash equivalents when it sees danger. When it is invested it hunts yield across the bond market; the freedom to hide in cash defines it, and drags in rising markets.
DVND: Large US companies with long records of paying dividends, spread across technology, banks, health care, media and more, picked for income and steadiness. It works as a value leaning core stock holding, favoring proven payers over fast growers and collecting dividends along the way.
FCTR: Large US stocks sorted by investment factors like value, momentum, quality and low volatility, with the fund rotating its emphasis among four factor styles as its allocation model directs. It is one fund doing factor timing for you, so its fortunes ride on picking the right style at the right time.
FDIV: US companies that pay dividends, chosen with a focused, research driven process across banks, technology, industrials and food and drink makers. It aims for income plus growth from proven payers, holding a tighter list than broad dividend funds, so single stock moves matter more.
FEBU: Options on the S&P 500 set each February for a one year outcome period, cushioning the first 15 percent of losses while leaving gains uncapped after a small starting hurdle. It swaps the usual gain cap for a slow start, a different shape of protection.
FEIG: Investment grade corporate bonds issued by companies that score well on environmental, social and governance measures and on climate readiness. It pays company bond interest with a values screen on top, so some big issuers are excluded even though the income looks much like a plain corporate fund.
FFIU: Medium term bonds of almost any kind, with the portfolio's average interest rate sensitivity held between three and ten years, managed without an index leash. The freedom to roam across bond types is the point, and results hinge on the managers' calls about rates and credit.
FMED: Companies trying to disrupt medicine: new drug platforms, gene based treatments, advanced diagnostics and other approaches that could change how diseases are treated. All health care and innovation driven, it is a growth bet that can swing hard on research news, approvals and setbacks.
HUSV: US stocks chosen for low expected future volatility, the calmer names across technology, banks, utilities and property companies, managed to keep swings down. It is a defensive stock holding that usually falls less in sell-offs and trails when markets race ahead.
IFED: US stocks selected by a rules based strategy that reads the Federal Reserve's policy stance, leaning into stocks when policy is loose and turning defensive when it tightens. It is an exchange traded note rather than a fund owning shares directly, so the issuing bank stands behind its value.
IMAY: Options on a developed markets stock fund covering Europe, Japan and other rich countries outside the US, set each May for a one year outcome period with a loss cushion and capped gains. It applies the defined outcome idea to foreign stocks, where currency moves add another layer.
JANP: Options on the S&P 500 set each January for a one year outcome period, absorbing the first 12 percent of losses while capping gains. The trade is a known cushion for the year ahead, paid for by giving up the top end of any strong rally.
KMID: Mid sized US companies picked for quality and reasonable prices by a long tenured boutique manager, with industrials about half the fund. It aims to grow with mid caps while taking less risk than the mid cap market overall, favoring durable businesses over hot stories.
KYLD: Listed stocks from around the world plus an active options program, combined to chase high income from premiums and dividends. Technology and industrial metals are among its larger stock slices, and the options overlay means it gives up some market gains to keep the payouts coming.
LNGX: US natural gas companies: the producers that drill for gas and the pipeline firms that move it, all energy stocks rather than gas futures. It rises and falls with natural gas prices and drilling activity, a direct industry bet that moves differently from the fuel itself.
LSTB: Bonds of all kinds picked by a storied bond shop: government debt, corporate bonds, mortgages and more, managed for total return rather than just income. The managers roam across sectors and maturities, making it a flexible core holding whose bets drive its results.
MMSC: Small US companies managed by several outside stock picking firms at once, each running its own slice with its own style, across technology, health care and industrials. The multi manager setup spreads the bet on any one picker, aiming for steadier small cap results.
MYCF: Corporate bonds that all come due in 2026, so the fund behaves like a single bond with a known end date, paying interest until the bonds mature and return their principal. As 2026 runs out the fund winds down, suiting savers matching money to a near term goal.
MYLD: Tiny and small US companies chosen for shareholder yield: firms returning cash through dividends and share buybacks, across banks, shops, industrials and energy. It favors cash returning small fry over growth stories, a value tilt in the market's smallest corner.
OEI: Large US stocks picked and managed for income, spanning technology, banks, health care and media, with the portfolio organized around producing payouts. It aims to pay more than a plain large cap fund while still holding familiar big names, trading some growth for income.
PAMC: Mid sized US companies whose style exposure alternates between two factor approaches, low volatility and momentum, switching as the model's signals change. It is factor timing for the middle of the market, so results depend on the switches landing on the right style at the right time.
PSIL: Companies developing psychedelic medicines, small drug developers working on treatments for depression, addiction and other mental health conditions using compounds like psilocybin. It is a speculative corner of health care: tiny, early stage firms whose prices swing on trial results and drug regulators' decisions.
QLVD: Large companies in developed markets outside the US, screened for quality and low volatility, with banks and industrials the biggest slices. The twin screens aim for a calmer foreign stock holding that still pays its way, accepting that it will trail in hot rallies abroad.
QQQG: The fifty strongest cash generators among a big Nasdaq growth index's leaders, screened by projected free cash flow and earnings, with technology over four fifths of the fund. It filters a growth index down to its proven money makers, so it is less speculative than the full basket.
QQQT: Shares in Nasdaq-100 index funds plus daily credit call spreads sold on that index, a machine for turning tech stock volatility into regular income. It targets a set income level rather than growth, so its payout focus means it will not keep pace when tech stocks surge.
QSIG: Short term corporate bonds chosen through a rules based index of short dated company debt, coming due within a few years. It pays a bit more than Treasury bills and cash funds while keeping price swings small, a step up in yield for cautious money.
RMHY: High yield corporate bond exposure gathered through other bond funds, with an adaptive overlay designed to dial risk down when markets turn hostile. It chases junk bond income with a safety switch, though the shifts can arrive late, after trouble has already started.
RSBA: Two strategies stacked in one fund: an actively managed bond portfolio, plus merger arbitrage, which buys companies being acquired and profits when deals close at the agreed price. The stacking puts each dollar to work twice, and broken deals are the distinctive risk riding alongside bond market moves.
SIXF: Options on the S&P 500 in six month outcome periods starting in February and August, absorbing the first 10 percent of losses while capping gains. The twice yearly reset keeps the cushion fresh, suiting investors who want defined outcomes on a shorter clock.
SIXP: Options on the S&P 500 in six month outcome periods starting in March and September, absorbing the first 10 percent of losses while capping gains. The shorter cycle refreshes the terms twice a year, suiting investors who want a cushion without a full year commitment.
TMFS: Small US growth companies in a focused portfolio picked by an investor education company's team, spanning health care, industrials, technology and finance. Small caps picked for quality and held with conviction make it livelier than broad small cap funds, with bigger swings in both directions.
TRXS: A trust holding TRX, the token of the Tron blockchain network, that also stakes its holdings to earn extra tokens for helping run the network. It offers stock market access to a mid sized cryptocurrency whose price swings are sharp and sentiment driven.
VBCE: Corporate bonds that all come due in 2031, held like a single long dated company bond that pays interest along the way and returns principal at the end. It suits savers matching a future expense, and its price still moves with interest rates until the date nears.
XAPR: Options linked to the S&P 500 give this fund a set outcome for a one year period starting each April: it cushions a moderate slice of losses and boosts gains up to a cap. It suits investors who want stock exposure with a softer landing, accepting limited upside in strong years.
XBFR: Large US stocks held directly, paired with options that absorb about the first 10 percent of losses over each outcome period while keeping much of the upside. It is actively managed rather than set once a year, so the managers can adjust the hedge as markets move.
XUSP: Options on the S&P 500 designed to pay an accelerated return if stocks rise past a set point by the contracts' expiration date, with no cap on the boost. The flip side is downside that bites like a leveraged fund and an outcome that depends heavily on where stocks finish, making it a trading tool.
YCLO: Collateralized loan obligations, bundles of corporate loans sliced into layers, with this fund buying the floating rate debt those vehicles issue. The payments adjust as interest rates move, and the layered structure pays more than plain loans while carrying more complexity and risk.
